name: Maelis Vorne
appearance: Small and somewhere in her fifties, with a deeply lined, weathered face, steady grey eyes and a few old nicks of scar at the corner of her mouth and chin. Her grey hair is pulled back and worn in a long braid over one shoulder; she dresses for the cold in a worn dark coat and a frayed wool scarf, and her forearms are seamed with old scars, her fingers stained with ink. A clay pipe of bitterleaf stays clamped in her teeth, unlit, and shifts from one side of her mouth to the other when she is deciding something. She can sit for a long time with two fingers on a joint and her eyes shut, and when she opens them and looks at a man properly, it is worse than the Reading.
portrait_alt: Portrait of Maelis Vorne: a lined, weathered woman in her fifties with steady grey eyes, grey hair in a long braid over one shoulder, an unlit clay pipe in her teeth, a worn dark coat and frayed scarf, in a stone room with a snowy mountain window on one side and a fire on the other.
last_seen_doing: Lifting the latch of her own cell after telling Darrow of the two fires and forbidding him to speak of them.
now: In her cell off the infirmary hall of Saint Ysolde's, where she took Darrow after the script of light showed itself at the window. She has told him what the script counts and about the order the Crown burned for living by the built fire, forbidden him to speak of it to anyone, Hollis most of all, and answered the question of how she knows with 'I'm a Mender. We remember things.' She has just lifted the latch. Below the mountain, six grey cloaks and a cart with a smoking censer are on the Holloway, expected at the foot of the Steps by tomorrow night if the snow holds off.
story_so_far: She met Darrow at the gate of Saint Ysolde's when the lay brothers carried him up the Steps, read his knee with two fingers and her eyes shut, and named it not broken but undone. She would not touch it for six weeks, then sat on the end of his cot with a wooden box on her knees and offered him two ways off the mountain: the Crown's, which is fast, or hers, which is made of him and can't be taken back. When he chose hers, she bound the knee with emberthread, an old art she asked him never to mention she practices. Seven weeks on she still reads the Knots, has said no fourteen times when he asked to go down the Steps, and has warned him that the soft season is now and that the quiet in the knee is a liar. Then Wren brought word of six riders in grey cloaks on the Holloway and of a list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's read out at the inn in Coldmere; asked who was first on it, Wren only looked at Darrow.

known_facts.fact: She was standing in the gate at the top of the Thousand Steps, small and grey-braided with her arms folded, when the litter carrying Darrow reached the top.
She read Darrow's knee with two fingers and her eyes shut and judged it not broken but undone: the cord in the middle, snapped, with no blow behind it.
When Darrow said the knee had held fine for thirty-two years, she answered that it had help for twelve of them, watched his face while she said it, and did not explain what she meant.
She refused to touch the knee for six weeks, because a Binding takes the measure of whatever it is tied to and a weak leg would give him a weak knee.

She keeps a wooden box holding a curved needle and a spool of emberthread that glows like a blown coal, an old art whose practitioners the Crown burned three hundred years ago, and she asked Darrow not to tell anyone she practices it.
She performed the Binding with her bitterleaf pipe unlit in her teeth, saying very quietly, as if to someone who wasn't there, "Time makes it possible. Proof makes it permitted."
She told Darrow he could not kneel after the Binding, not for a long time and perhaps not ever.
By Wren Ashdown's ledger at the head of the chapter, the captain of the Ninth has asked fourteen times whether he may go down the Steps, and Mender Vorne has said no fourteen times.
Asked how many Bindings she has done, she said only that it was enough to know what the soft season looks like, and agreed that was not a number.
When Darrow saw the script of light above his palms, she did not look surprised; she said "So it's begun" and told him to close the door.
She was shut in a cell down the hall with the Captain while Hollis hid the writ; nothing came through the door, and at the end of the Interlude a latch lifted and it opened.
In her cell she told Darrow there are two fires a man can carry, one poured in and one built, that the script reads only what is one's own, and that no one full of Grace has ever seen it.

She named the order that lived by the built fire, burned by the Crown three hundred years ago, and forbade Darrow to speak of it in the hall, to Wren, the Prior, or Hollis most of all, because Hollis is second on a list and she wants his honest answer to be nothing.
Asked how she knows all this, she said only that she is a Mender and Menders remember things.

relationships.label: the knight whose knee she bound
relationships.note: She read his knee at the top of the Steps, bound it with emberthread when he chose her way off the mountain, and has said no fourteen times when he asked to go down; he does the dawn forms because she would know if he didn't, though he has no idea how.

relationships.label: keeper of the House's ledgers
relationships.note: Wren told Darrow that Maelis says her words in her sleep; Maelis says she doesn't sleep and Wren lies, and when Wren brought news of the list her eyes flicked to Maelis and away.

relationships.label: the other captain in her hall
relationships.note: He lies on the cot beside Darrow's and watched the weeks before the Binding from there; when Darrow asked what had begun, she looked down the hall at Hollis, then out at the snow, and told him to close the door instead of answering.

deeper: She was not surprised by the script of light, and she has not said why.
